{{Short description|Removal of points from a manifold}}
{{distinguish|Puncturing (coding theory)}}

In [[topology]], '''puncturing''' a [[manifold]] is removing a [[finite set]] of [[point (topology)|points]] from that manifold.{{sfn|Seifert|Threlfall|1980|p=29}} The set of points can be small as a single point. In this case, the manifold is known as '''once-punctured'''. With the removal of a second point, it becomes '''twice-punctured''', and so on.

Examples of punctured manifolds include the [[disk (mathematics)|open disk]] (which is a [[sphere]] with a single puncture), the [[cylinder (geometry)|cylinder]] (which is a sphere with two punctures),{{sfn|Seifert|Threlfall|1980|p=29}} and the [[Möbius strip]] (which is a [[projective plane]] with a single puncture).{{sfn|Seifert|Threlfall|1980|p=12}}

The set of non-zero [[complex number]]s is the [[complex plane]] once punctured at the origin, sometimes denoted <math>\Complex^*</math>.<ref name="e030">{{cite web | title=C^* -- from Wolfram MathWorld | publisher=Wolfram Research, Inc. | date=2001-11-15 | url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/C-Star.html | access-date=2026-04-14}}</ref>
